enrichment.short_title: Asylum internal relocation in Iraqi Kurdistan
key_facts: An Iraqi Kurdish asylum seeker from Halabja was accepted as credible and as having a well-founded fear of persecution by the IMIK in his home area.
The adjudicator dismissed his appeal on the basis that he could safely relocate within the Kurdish Autonomous Region where the IMIK had no influence.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal, and the claimant sought judicial review.
The Secretary of State gave an undertaking that Kurdish returnees would not be sent to northern Iraq unless safe and not via Baghdad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal to grant leave to appeal against an adjudicator's asylum decision.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where an asylum seeker has a well-founded fear in one part of his country but could reasonably relocate to a safe part without undue harshness, a decision maker may adopt a holistic Refugee Convention analysis rather than treating the fear test and protection test as wholly separate hurdles; current lack of safe access to northern Iraq did not automatically confer refugee status if internal relocation remained viable once safe return became possible.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator misdirected herself on internal relocation and the Refugee Convention
Whether lack of current safe access to northern Iraq entitled the claimant to refugee status
Whether the IAT should have granted leave to appeal on obvious grounds
Whether the adjudicator failed to consider relevant country evidence

linked_authorities: R v Home Secretary ex parte Robinson

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on internal relocation law with clear outcome and extensive authority discussion.

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan asylum JR after LTTE confession
key_facts: A Sri Lankan Tamil claimant was detained, beaten, and forced to sign a confession of LTTE membership before being released on payment of a bribe and leaving Sri Lanka the next day.
The adjudicator accepted the primary facts but inferred that the authorities had no continuing interest in him and dismissed the asylum appeal.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal, treating the adjudicator's inference as unchallengeable.
The Court of Appeal had recently held in Selvaratnam that a signed LTTE confession created a substantial risk of continuing interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal to grant leave to appeal against an adjudicator's asylum and human rights decision.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review succeeded; the IAT determination was quashed and remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator accepts that a credible asylum seeker signed a confession of LTTE membership but infers, without adequate explanation, that no record or continuing interest exists, that reasoning is susceptible to properly arguable challenge; the IAT must apply the real-prospect-of-success test under Rule 18(7) with anxious scrutiny and cannot treat such inferences as unassailable.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT applied the correct test for granting leave to appeal
Whether the adjudicator's inference about continuing authority interest was sustainable
Whether a signed LTTE confession meant the claimant remained of interest to the authorities
Whether relief should be refused because leave would inevitably have been refused anyway
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State ex parte Saleem

confidence.notes: Clear first-instance reasoning on IAT leave test and confession evidence with recent Court of Appeal authority directly in point.

enrichment.short_title: IHT business property relief for caravan site shares
key_facts: The deceased held 85% of the shares in Dunton Park Caravan Sites Limited, which operated residential and touring caravan sites and ancillary services.
The Special Commissioner held the company's business was not wholly or mainly one of making or holding investments, so the shares qualified for 100% business property relief.
The Inland Revenue appealed, arguing site fees and storage fees were exploitation of land as investment property.
Profits from site fees, storage, and utility resale substantially exceeded those from the country club and caravan sales.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a Special Commissioner's decision on inheritance tax business property relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the shareholding did not qualify for relief because the company's main business was holding investments in land.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 105(3) IHTA 1984, holding land to produce a return from licensing site use and storage is a business of holding investments, and ancillary profitable services such as utility resale are part of that investment business; once investment and non-investment activities are separated, a qualitative assessment shows where holding investments is the company's very business rather than merely incidental.
legal_issues: Whether site fees and caravan storage constituted holding investments in land
Whether ancillary services were severable non-investment activities
Whether the business consisted wholly or mainly of making or holding investments
Whether the Special Commissioner erred by applying Cook v Medway before identifying the investment business
linked_authorities: Tootal Broadhurst Lee Co Ltd v IRC
Cook v Medway Housing Society Ltd
The Governors of the Rotunda Hospital v Coman

confidence.notes: Structured tax judgment applying established Weston methodology to detailed business facts.

enrichment.short_title: Void gift of house share for lack of capacity

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: John Williams, a man with significant learning disability and functional illiteracy, inherited his mother's house outright in 1986.
In 1987 he executed a deed of gift conveying the property to himself, his brother George, and sister-in-law Marion as tenants in common in 50:25:25 shares so they would move in and support him.

George and Marion gave up secure council accommodation in reliance on the transfer, but John's solicitors failed to give him the extensive plain-English explanation required for his level of disability.
Expert evidence showed John could understand only if the transaction were explained over many hours and tested in his own words.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for declaration that a deed of gift was void or voidable, with alternative claims for undue influence and an order for sale under TOLATA 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Gift held void for lack of capacity and procured by undue influence; defendants' change-of-position and voidable-gift defences rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Where a donor's only asset of substantial value is given away by deed into joint ownership on trust for sale, he must understand the general nature and effect of the transaction, including the implications of tenants in common ownership; if a prima facie case of incapacity is raised and the evidence shows adequate explanation was required but not given, the burden shifts to the donees to prove capacity, and a gift lacking capacity is void rather than merely voidable.
legal_issues: Whether John had capacity to execute the deed of gift
What degree of understanding Re Beaney requires for a gift of one's only substantial asset
Whether the gift was procured by undue influence
Whether change of position or voidable-gift principles limited relief

Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2)
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No 2)
The Special Trustees for Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children v Rushin

confidence.notes: Long fact-sensitive judgment with clear legal conclusions on capacity, burden of proof, and relief.

enrichment.short_title: Murder joint enterprise after doormen feud
key_facts: Stephen Cole was attacked and hacked to death by a large group of Liverpool doormen at the Farmer's Arms after a feud involving John Dillon.
McCarthy admitted joining the convoy and being present in the alcove but denied participating in the armed attack.
Blood from McCarthy and the deceased was found in the alcove; McCarthy fled to Wales and disposed of bloodstained clothing.
The jury convicted McCarthy of murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction by leave of the full court, challenging the trial judge's joint-enterprise summing up.
enrichment.ratio: On facts where many attackers were armed with bladed weapons pursuant to a plan to do serious harm, a secondary party who participated in the attack must have foreseen use of such weapons; Powell and English does not require a separate direction that the secondary party must have been aware of each weapon where the scale of the armed mob and his proximity to the killing made such awareness inevitable once participation was found.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately directed the jury under R v Powell and English
Whether the appellant had to be aware others had bladed weapons to be guilty of murder
Whether the summing up wrongly treated presence alone as sufficient
Whether a departure from the common design affected liability

confidence.notes: Focused criminal appeal with clear application of joint-enterprise principles to distinctive mob-attack facts.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair dismissal remedies for pregnant employee
key_facts: Mrs Shepherd, a high-performing sales executive, was dismissed for redundancy while pregnant after a sham selection process motivated by her pregnancy.
Liability for unfair dismissal and sex discrimination was found and not appealed.
The tribunal awarded about £191,000 including two and a half years' future earnings loss and ten years' future pension loss.
The employer challenged the pension period, the 5% accelerated-receipt discount, and interest on the gross award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on quantum of compensatory award.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partly allowed; pension loss period upheld, accelerated-receipt discount remitted, and interest held payable only on the net sum.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal may make a broad-brush award for long-term pension loss where uncontradicted mitigation evidence supports it, but a conventional 5% discount for accelerated receipt is an annual rate and cannot be applied once to a combined multi-year earnings and pension award; interest compensates for being kept out of money actually received and should not be calculated on gross sums deducted for tax and NIC.
legal_issues: Whether ten years' future pension loss was perverse
Whether the tribunal misapplied the 5% accelerated-receipt discount
Whether interest should be awarded on gross or net compensation
Whether an appellate court may interfere with tribunal assessments of future loss
index_terms: York Trailer Company Ltd v Sparkes
linked_authorities: York Trailer Company Ltd v Sparkes

confidence.notes: Clear Court of Appeal judgment on three distinct remedy points with supporting authority.

enrichment.short_title: Restrictive covenant after ACT sale to iSOFT
key_facts: iSOFT bought ACT, a UK laboratory information systems business, from Misys under an agreement containing three-year non-compete and customer-solicitation restrictions.
Clause 11.4 allowed Misys to acquire competing businesses employing up to 20% of staff in the restricted area, subject to an offer-to-sell procedure to iSOFT.
Misys later acquired Sunquest and its UK subsidiary Europa, which competed with iSOFT for the West London Pathology Consortium contract.
Negotiations to sell Europa to iSOFT failed, and iSOFT sued for specific performance and an injunction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court refusal of specific performance and injunctive relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both specific performance and injunction issues.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 11.4.2 required an indication of willingness to sell at fair market value followed by good-faith negotiation, not an immediately binding offer capable of acceptance; such a process was too uncertain for specific performance because the court would have to construct an entire share-and-licence contract from scratch, and clause 11.4 implicitly permitted an acquired target business and its parent to continue their ordinary commercial relationship without breaching clause 11.2.
legal_issues: Whether clause 11.4.2 required an offer capable of immediate acceptance
Whether the clause was sufficiently certain for specific performance
Whether Misys breached clause 11.2 by assisting Europa after acquiring Sunquest
How clause 11.4 interacts with the non-compete restrictions
linked_authorities: Hillas & Co Ltd v Arcos Ltd
Didymi Corporation v Atlantic Lines and Navigation Co Inc

confidence.notes: Detailed commercial construction judgment with agreed facts and clear conclusions on both issues.

key_facts: The Westgate Partnership applied to redevelop the Westgate Centre in Oxford with major retail, residential, office, and transport uses.
Oxford City Council supported the scheme and an inspector recommended approval, but the Secretary of State called in the application and refused permission.
The refusal rested heavily on harm to the historic conservation area and Oxford skyline, especially the City Edge block.
The claimants challenged the decision letter for failing properly to address development plan conformity, PPG6, and retail need.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 applications to quash the Secretary of State's refusal of outline and ancillary planning permissions after a public inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Applications allowed; the Secretary of State's decision was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an inspector recommends approval after balancing benefits and conservation harm, the Secretary of State must clearly decide and give reasons on principal controversial issues such as development plan conformity, PPG6 sequential-test compliance, and retail need; noting an inspector's favourable conclusion without stating agreement or reasoned disagreement, or expressing reservations unsupported by evidence, renders the decision letter legally defective and prevents a proper balancing exercise.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State adequately determined development plan conformity under section 54A
Whether he decided the PPG6 sequential test and retail need/economic impact issues
Whether his conservation and townscape objections were supported by evidence
Whether deficiencies in the decision letter caused substantial prejudice

enrichment.short_title: Former Swift CEO allowed as hire-rate expert
key_facts: After a road traffic accident, the defendant sought to rely on an Autofocus expert report by Colin McLean on reasonable prestige-car hire rates.
McLean had been Chief Executive of Swift Rent-a-Car Limited, the hire company used by the claimants, for five months in 1999.
A district judge permitted the report, but a circuit judge set it aside because justice could not be seen to be done.
Factortame (No 8) subsequently disapproved using the apparent-bias test for expert admissibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a county court case management decision excluding expert evidence in a fast-track credit-hire claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; permission to rely on Mr McLean's report was reinstated.
enrichment.ratio: The test for excluding expert evidence is not apparent bias but whether the expert has relevant expertise and can fulfil the primary duty to the court despite any interest or past connection; a former executive relationship with a hire company used in the claim does not automatically disqualify an expert, though it may affect the weight of his evidence and costs.
legal_issues: Whether past employment by an interested hire company tainted expert evidence
Whether the apparent-bias test applied to expert witness admissibility
What case management factors under the overriding objective govern expert evidence on the fast track
Whether Mr McLean had the requisite expertise and independence
linked_authorities: Liverpool Roman Catholic Archdiocese Trustees Incorporated v Goldberg (No 2)
Regina Factortame Ltd v Secretary of State for Transport (No 8)

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural judgment applying post-Factortame expert-evidence principles to concrete facts.

enrichment.short_title: Lease forfeiture after patisserie user breach

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: The tenants used a leased patisserie premises to prepare and sell hot and cold food for on- and off-premises consumption, breaching a Class A1 user covenant.
The landlord sought possession, mesne profits, reimbursement of drain repair costs, and legal fees under the lease.
The tenants argued waiver or estoppel, contending the landlord knew of and encouraged their catering use and a kitchen extension.
The judge found the landlord knew of hot-food sales but not on-site commercial cooking, and that common drain works required apportionment by the landlord's surveyor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Tenant appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court order granting possession, mesne profits, costs, and repair contributions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed except on drain apportionment; the £1,113.58 repair contribution and related interest were set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Waiver or estoppel by acquiescence requires a clear representation that strict user rights will not be enforced and detrimental reliance; awareness of some covenant breaches and rent acceptance does not necessarily extend to sanctioning on-site cooking, and a lease requiring a fair proportion of drain expenses to be ascertained by the landlord's surveyor cannot be satisfied by a solicitor acting in a surveying role.
legal_issues: Whether the landlord waived or was estopped from enforcing the user covenant
Whether drain repair contributions had been validly ascertained under the lease
Whether the landlord's repairing covenant covered common drains
Whether mesne profits, legal costs, and interest were payable
linked_authorities: Woodhouse AC Israel Cocoa SA v Nigerian Produce Manufacturing Co
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd

confidence.notes: Multiple issues on appeal but core fact findings on waiver and lease construction are clearly recorded.
